claims.text: The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with uniformly dispersed Mg, Ti, and Zn.
Service-like thermal exposure drives Ti and Zn out of the metastable solid solution by diffusion.
Diffusing Ti and Zn segregate and coalesce into intermetallic phases during thermal aging.
Mg-Ti-Zn multi-principal-element alloys can contain Ti2Zn and other intermetallic phases.
Thermal exposure forms an interconnected network of intermetallic compounds.
Fine, discontinuously distributed intermetallic phases nucleate a protective TiO2-rich surface film.
A TiO2-rich surface film enhances passivation and lowers corrosion current density in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys.
Coarsening intermetallics into a continuous network enhances microgalvanic coupling with the Mg matrix.
Microgalvanic coupling between intermetallic phases and the Mg matrix undermines passivation and accelerates corrosion.
A fine, dispersed intermetallic population can retain or enhance corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
A contiguous, coarsened intermetallic structure reduces corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Fine intermetallic phases and their associated TiO2-rich film retain or enhance high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The as-processed metastable alloy has moderate corrosion resistance without significant intermetallic-phase development.
Temperatures of 200–400°C in oxidizing atmospheres are sufficient to trigger the proposed diffusion and intermetallic evolution.
Mg-Ti-Zn alloys have a demonstrated tendency to form intermetallic compounds, including Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25.
The combined effects of Ti and Zn in bulk Mg-rich multi-element alloys, including phase stability and passivation behavior, remain poorly understood.
There is a critical intermetallic size or connectivity threshold separating beneficial passivation from detrimental galvanic behavior.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis initially states that thermal exposure forms an interconnected intermetallic network, whereas the beneficial branch requires the thermally evolved phases to remain fine and discontinuous. The proposed sequence does not clearly distinguish an early discontinuous stage from the later interconnected stage.
